_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC SS4
concept_redesign_note: The approved concept specified Option B as a ground-standing cylindrical 'standpipe.' Case-research found no public, comparably rigorous cost/area dataset pairing a spherical elevated tank against a ground standpipe specifically. It DID find something better: a real, professional-engineer-sealed 2019 Black & Veatch cost study (for the City of Lawrence, Kansas) directly comparing a spheroid elevated tank against a multi-column elevated tank -- a cylindrical tank on multiple support legs -- at the identical site, capacity, and overflow height, with real fabricator quotes for both. This is the SPEC-preferred 'redesign' exit under case-research's NOT-FOUND procedure (skills/case-research/SKILL.md Section 5.2/worked example): swap the unsourceable pairing for a real, rigorously comparable one that preserves the concept's actual pedagogical target (sphere vs. cylinder, same volume, real cost tension between less-area-but-costlier-to-build vs. more-area-but-cheaper-to-build). Every dollar and area figure in this case is now real and cited (see sources[] S5-S16), rather than a mix of real spheroid data and an invented standpipe cost. Flagged here for the project owner per pipeline doctrine on any structural deviation from an approved concept.
readiness_revision_note: A 2026-09-06 case-readiness QA pass (cold-solve, both-sides, and twist probes, independently) found this case's original balance defective: the Multi-Column won every dollar metric (capital cost, 60-year lifecycle cost, cost/gallon) at every capacity, and the twist probe showed this win is mathematically invariant across a +/-50% capacity range (both designs' costs scale by the same capacity^(2/3) law). Argument A as originally written (future regulatory exposure) was real but speculative and did not constitute a genuine present-day dilemma. FIX (case-write level, per PIPELINE.md 'QA BLOCKER on structure/balance -> re-enter at case-write'): re-read the same real Black & Veatch source memo already used for S5-S16 and found a second real, present-day, sourced factor already present in that document but not yet used -- fabricator competition / sole-source procurement risk (new source S17, new case.md Appendix G, new Challenge 2c). The Spheroid has 3 qualified fabricators; the Multi-Column has exactly 1 (Caldwell Tanks), and the real engineering firm's own memo names this as 'added risk ... due to lack of competition.' This is not a fabricated balancing factor -- it was sitting in the same real, already-cited source document. No sourced dollar figure was altered; case.json.balance.margin_pct remains the real, computed 14.0% on the primary (dollar) metric, and the case's balance now rests on that dollar axis (B wins) plus this second real procurement-risk axis (A wins), matching how real municipal infrastructure decisions are actually made. Separately, this same pass corrected three real citation defects found by a Tier 2 data-decay probe: S2 (dropped an unsupported '3,300 connections' claim, replaced source), S3 (replaced a mis-cited CA Elections Code SS9401 -- which actually governs the mailed tax-rate disclosure statement, not bond-amount format -- with the correct CA Government Code SS43610), and S4 (replaced a dead USGS link with a live NIST Handbook 133 Appendix E citation). See RESEARCH_LOG.md for full detail and QA_REPORT.md for the re-run Tier 1/Tier 2 verdicts.

deliverables.text: A solved-dimensions sheet: starting from the required storage capacity in Appendix A, algebraically solve for the unknown dimension of each idealized reservoir shape -- the Spheroid's radius, using the sphere volume formula, and the Multi-Column's cylinder height, using the cylinder volume formula and the real tank diameter in Appendix C -- showing every step of the rearrangement, with a labeled sketch of each shape.

A surface-area comparison table: the idealized total exterior surface area of each reservoir shape (sphere: 4*pi*r^2; cylinder: 2*pi*r^2 + 2*pi*r*h), computed from the dimensions found in D1, in square feet.

A steel-area-per-gallon rate for each idealized design -- total surface area from D2 divided by the required capacity from Appendix A -- expressed in square feet per 1,000 gallons, with the unit conversion shown.

A real-world cost-per-square-foot calculation for each design: Appendix D's sourced total construction (capital) cost divided by Appendix B/C's sourced real fabricated exterior area for that design, plus a written paragraph explaining why this real per-square-foot rate comes out different for the two designs even though both are welded, coated steel construction.

An original visual display (a bar chart or equivalent) comparing each design's total 60-year lifecycle cost per gallon of capacity from Appendix D, plus one sentence stating the single construction-bond dollar figure recommended for the ballot.

balance.argument_a: The Spheroid has three real, qualified fabricators at this capacity (McDermott, Caldwell Tanks, Landmark Structures) [S17], while the Multi-Column has exactly one (Caldwell Tanks) [S17] -- a real, present-day procurement fact from the same professional-engineer-sealed memo that supplies every cost figure in this case, not a speculative future risk. The real engineering firm's own memo states plainly that sole-sourcing the Multi-Column means 'no opportunity for competitive bidding,' and its own final Recommendations section names this as 'added risk ... due to lack of competition' [S17] -- the same real firm that produced the cost numbers B relies on is on record treating this as a genuine reason to hesitate on the Multi-Column, regardless of its lower sticker price. For a town six weeks into a boil-water advisory racing a Friday ballot deadline, a design that cannot be competitively bid carries real exposure to price and schedule risk that a single lifecycle-cost figure does not capture. A's case does not require winning the dollar metric (see 'The margin') -- it rests on a different, equally real and sourced axis: which design the town can actually procure competitively.
balance.argument_b: The Multi-Column's simpler, non-specialized steel fabrication is dramatically cheaper to build per square foot ($54.81/sq ft, derived from S13/S11) than the Spheroid's curved-knuckle single-shaft design ($124.12/sq ft, derived from S7/S5) -- more than twice as cheap per square foot -- and that capital-cost advantage more than offsets the Multi-Column's larger area and higher 60-year recoating bill (S14 vs S8). Under the case's own real, sourced numbers, B wins on the graded dollar metric by a real but thin 14.0% margin: $2.78/gal [S16] against the Spheroid's $3.23/gal [S10] -- and this margin is stable across a wide range of capacity choices (case.json.qa.tier2.P5), so it is not a fragile artifact of the 750,000-gallon scenario choice. B's real case is that a documented, quantified savings of roughly $339,000 in total 60-year lifecycle cost (S15 vs S9) is worth accepting a real but unquantified sole-source procurement risk (Appendix G) for -- a genuine, defensible dollars-vs-risk trade a town facing an active boil-water advisory and a hard Friday deadline could reasonably make either way.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |cost_per_gallon(A) - cost_per_gallon(B)| / max(cost_per_gallon(A), cost_per_gallon(B)), using each option's real, sourced 60-year total lifecycle cost per gallon (S10, S16): A = $3.23/gal, B = $2.78/gal. margin = |3.23 - 2.78| / 3.23 = 0.45 / 3.23 = 13.93%, rounded to 14.0%. Both figures come from the same real 2019 engineering cost study (Table 2-5) at the same 0.75 MG capacity, so this is a genuine, apples-to-apples comparison, not an artifact of mismatched assumptions. This 14.0% figure describes only the PRIMARY (dollar) metric, on which B wins outright and invariantly across capacity (confirmed by three independent Tier 2 probes -- cold-solve, both-sides, and twist -- during the original QA pass); it does NOT by itself make this a balanced dilemma, since B also wins every other dollar metric (capital cost, 60-year lifecycle cost) at every capacity. The case's actual balance -- both options genuinely defensible per SPEC SS2 -- rests on a SECOND, real, sourced, non-dollar axis added during a QA-driven case-write revision (2026-09-06): Appendix G's fabricator-competition data (S17), on which A has a genuine, present-day, structural advantage (3 qualified bidders vs. 1) that the same real engineering firm treats as a real reason for caution. SCOPE CAVEAT (added after a Tier 2 twist-integrity probe, 2026-09-06): S17's fabricator counts are sourced specifically 'at 0.5-0.75 MG capacity' -- unlike the dollar-cost invariance finding above, which sensitivity_model.py confirms holds across a +/-50% capacity sweep, Appendix G's fabricator counts are NOT independently verified outside the 0.5-0.75 MG band the source memo evaluated, and this case's own required capacity (0.75 MG) sits at the edge of that range. The two findings must not be conflated -- see case.md Appendix G's 'Scope note' and FACILITATOR.md Socratic Question 7. NOTE: the concept sheet named a 6-10% target range for the dollar metric; the real sourced data lands at 14.0%, still comfortably inside SPEC SS2's 20% hard cap and consistent with this corpus's typical 10-15% band (e.g. cases/the-deferred-repair at 13.0%).

modeling_assumptions.basis: A real spheroid tank has a flared cone base and central access shaft a pure sphere formula does not capture; a real multi-column tank's 'outside area' includes its support legs. No public source reduces either real design to pure geometric primitives.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not change which design wins the graded cost comparison -- it only explains the expected gap between a Hero's own D1/D2 arithmetic and Appendix B/C's real figures.
